structure.title: Defining justice
structure.text: Books 1–4 move from failed definitions to a city built in discussion as a way to examine the soul.

structure.title: Education and testing
structure.text: Books 5–10 examine rulers, knowledge, damaged constitutions, poetry, and the stakes of choosing a life.

people.name: Socrates
people.text: Socrates, who is asked at a dinner party in Piraeus what justice is, and who ends up describing an ideal city to find out.

people.name: Glaucon and Adeimantus
people.text: Plato's brothers, who want Socrates to prove that justice is good for its own sake, even for someone who could act unjustly and never be caught.

people.name: Thrasymachus
people.text: A sophist who bursts into the conversation insisting that justice is simply whatever serves the stronger, and that only fools obey it.

context.title: A spoken investigation
context.text: Speakers propose models and encounter objections. An argument's presence in the dialogue does not remove the need to assess it.
context.takeaway: Follow the objection as well as the proposal.

context.title: City and soul
context.text: The city's divisions help Socrates describe competing elements within a person. The analogy does considerable argumentative work.

notice.why: The proposed guardians' virtue depends partly on controlling their surroundings.

notice.text: Track changes in the meaning of justice.
notice.why: A definition can quietly shift as the scale changes.

opening: Imagine a ring that lets its owner become invisible. With punishment removed, why would anyone remain just? Plato refuses to let Socrates answer with a reassuring speech about being good. He has to defend justice against people who suspect morality is a bargain the weak impose on the strong. The argument grows into a proposed city whose rulers control education, poetry, and family life. Following it means watching an attempt to secure human goodness acquire powers that should make its readers uneasy.
